turns.q: so where do I actually take the rate risk down — is it the tlt line, or is it one of those names? and what does that cost me
turns.answer:
On this book, the cleanest way to take rate risk down is the explicit TLT line, not one of the equities: TLT is already the dedicated rates instrument, while the equities are only measured rate proxies. By weight, the book’s biggest rate-risk proxy exposures sit in MSFT 16.1%, JPM 14.9%, AAPL 14.7%, LLY 12.7%, and GOOGL 12.5%; TLT itself is lower in the stack at 6.06%, and NVDA is the smallest of the ten at 4.24%. That means if you want to reduce the book’s rate exposure without changing the equity book’s shape much, TLT is the obvious lever; if you cut one of the names, you are reducing rate sensitivity only incidentally and also changing sector/issuer exposure.
What it costs you depends on which lever you pull. Reducing TLT lowers the book’s explicit duration and also removes a 6.06% weight 6.06%, but it does not tell you which equity beta you gave up. Reducing an equity name gives you a bigger trade-off: you cut both that name’s rate sensitivity and its own business exposure, with MSFT 16.1% and JPM 14.9% offering the most rate-risk to remove among the equities on a simple weight basis, while NVDA 4.24% is not the place to start if your goal is rate-risk reduction specifically. The desk’s fit is decent but not perfect — model R² is 80.8% on 750 observations, with max VIF 16.62× — so I would read this as a ranking of where the measured rate burden sits, not as a guarantee that the next dollar you trim comes with exactly the same sensitivity.
On the story question: NVDA is rate-sensitive, but it is not the book’s rate trade. If you mean the stock people usually cite when they say growth is long duration, the book’s own ordering puts MSFT, JPM, AAPL, LLY, and GOOGL ahead of NVDA on the rate-risk proxy weights 16.1% through 12.5%, with NVDA last 4.24%. So the narrative is partly true in the abstract, but in this book NVDA is more of a rate-sensitive growth name than the canonical rate trade.

turns.q: forget the restatement then. what would tell me first that they've stretched it too far — and at what level do I actually start worrying?
turns.answer:
The first thing I’d watch is whether the business still earns enough per dollar of revenue to absorb the reinvestment: for Microsoft that ratio is 30.5% (30.55% capex intensity over 2025-04-01..2026-03-31), for Amazon it is 20.3% (20.33%), and for Google I do not yet hold the comparable figure. If depreciation lives have been stretched too far, the early warning is not the depreciation line itself but a deterioration in the underlying operating mix: capex intensity keeps rising while asset turnover fails to improve, and gross margin no longer offsets it. On that read, Microsoft’s gross margin is 68.3% (68.31% over 2025-04-01..2026-03-31) and Amazon’s gross margin is an absence on this desk because gross_profit is not held for AMZN, so I cannot rank Amazon on margin quality from this line alone.
What level should make you start worrying: not a formula threshold from this desk, but a pattern. I would start paying attention when the reinvestment share is rising into the same period that asset turnover stalls or falls, because then the apparent profit is increasingly relying on a longer useful-life assumption rather than faster asset productivity. For the two names I can read today, Amazon’s asset turnover 0.81× (0.81x) is better than Microsoft’s 0.46× (0.458x), so Microsoft’s reported earnings are the ones more dependent on extracting more revenue from a heavier asset base; Amazon has the lower reinvestment share but the desk still lacks the gross-profit line needed to judge margin cushion.
So, in plain terms: I’d worry first when capex intensity keeps climbing and the asset-turnover line stops doing enough work to carry it; that is the earliest clue that depreciation may be too generous. If you want a cleaner tripwire for these three, the next step is to pull Google’s comparable operating mix and Amazon’s gross-profit line, then compare all three on the same basis instead of leaving one name as an absence.

turns.q: so if the rate flattens out from here, what does that do to the growth I'm underwriting?
turns.answer:
If the tax rate flattens from here, the growth you underwrite will lean more on pretax expansion and less on tax relief. On the latest 12-month window, pretax income is $25.73B and net income is $20.64B; the gap between them is $5.09B. The tax burden is 80.2%, while net margin is 31.7%, so taxes are still a meaningful bridge from pretax to after-tax, but not the whole bridge.
What is doing the most work is the pretax line itself: pretax income has grown much faster than the tax burden has changed, so a flat tax rate would remove a tailwind but would not erase the core earnings growth. The reading that changes most if the tax rate stops improving is the after-tax conversion, not the underlying earnings trajectory.

turns.q: and where does that cash actually sit
turns.answer:
Apple’s cash sits in more than just cash. The filing says AAPL’s balances of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities totaled [10-K Item 7], and the balance sheet shows cash and equivalents alone at $45.57B. The same filing breaks the pool into cash, money market funds, mutual funds, and marketable debt securities, split into current and non-current buckets.
So the answer is: a lot of it sits in marketable securities, not idle bank cash. The filing says those marketable debt securities are classified as current or non-current based on each instrument’s maturity, and that they are accounted for as available-for-sale. It also notes some amounts were restricted or held in escrow in prior periods, so not every dollar is freely deployable at every date.
What this means for the earlier point: net cash is cash plus liquid investments netted against debt. Gross debt still counts because the notes and commercial paper are real claims, and the filing separately discloses outstanding fixed-rate notes and commercial paper in the debt note.

The Company utilizes several outsourcing partners to manufacture subassemblies for the Company’s products and to perform final assembly and testing of finished products. turns.q: google files that risk section every year and it's basically a novel by now. what's actually different in this one — what did they add, and did anything quietly come out?
turns.answer:
The latest filing does add a few things, but the biggest change is not a fresh risk so much as a heavier emphasis on AI and the infrastructure needed to support it. In Item 1, Alphabet now frames itself as an “AI-first company,” says its “AI-optimized infrastructure” is a “key differentiator,” and notes that all 15 half-billion-user products use Gemini models; it also says Google Search has become a “dynamic, multimodal experience” with AI Overviews and AI Mode. In Item 7, management says 2025 and 2026 capex are being pushed higher for technical infrastructure, servers, network equipment, and data centers, and that AI offerings will require more compute power than historical offerings. In Item 1A, the new or newly sharpened risk language follows the same thread: AI is reshaping advertising, new monetization may differ from the historical model, and the company is signing significant leasing arrangements and large long-duration commercial agreements tied to compute capacity. The filing also now explicitly says Google Cloud’s business with financial services, healthcare, and public sector customers may bring added regulatory compliance, audit, cost-review, and sovereign-operating risks.
What looks quietly removed is not a cleanly labeled risk-factor deletion, but rather a softer pivot in the story. The filing still says more than 70% of 2025 revenue came from online advertising, yet the narrative now puts much more weight on cloud, subscriptions, platforms, devices, and AI products growing faster and becoming a larger share of revenue. That suggests the company is still dependent on ads, but it is spending more of the risk narrative on the transition path away from a pure ad story. I do not have a held line item here that proves an Item 1A sentence was deleted versus merely reworded, so the desk cannot call a specific omission beyond saying the year’s emphasis shifted toward AI, infrastructure, and diversified monetization. The desk also does not hold a filing-comparison diff for every risk-factor sentence, so a precise “what came out” list is absent unless you want me to compare against last year’s Item 1A text directly.
If you want the hard version, I can compare this 10-K against the prior year’s Item 1A and Item 7 to isolate added, removed, and rephrased risk language sentence by sentence. turns.q: if their table and the tape disagree, which one do I go with for a position we actually hold? and what would you need to see to change that
turns.answer:
For a position we actually hold, I would go with the book/tape reconciliation first, not the bank’s own rate table by itself: the table is management’s sensitivity framing, while the tape tells you what the market has already been pricing. On JPM, the tape has not been indifferent — its 1y return versus TLT is 21.7%, and it has been close to its high, with distance from the 52-week high at -1.79% as of 2026-09-04. That says the market has already done some work for you; it does not prove the table is wrong, but it does mean the table is not the only input.
What would change that reading is a new fact that the tape is no longer confirming the table’s regime: a material widening in JPM’s price-relative-to-TLT relationship, a break below the recent high-water mark after the table was published, or filing text showing the rate sensitivity only applies under conditions that are not the ones the market is trading. Right now I can point to JPM’s momentum being positive at 23.3% and its one-year volatility at 22.3%, but those answer momentum and noise, not whether the table’s shock assumption is currently the binding driver for the position.
So the practical rule is: use the filing table for scenario mechanics, use the tape for timing and confirmation, and if they disagree, treat that as a prompt to check whether the market has already moved past the scenario or whether the filing’s scenario was never meant to be linear. I cannot say the filing table is right or wrong here because I have not yet pulled the table itself in this turn; if you want, I can read the filing text and the rate table next and show exactly what the sensitivity says, then line that up against TLT behavior.

turns.q: forget sectors for a minute. is there one risk that turns up in three or four of these filings at once? because that's the thing that takes us out on the same day
turns.answer:
Yes — the common same-day risk across several of these filings is regulatory / government action risk, especially around antitrust, privacy, export controls, and other restrictions that can hit operations and trading in one go. In AAPL, the filing says the business can be materially affected by “increasing regulation, government investigations, legal actions and penalties” and by antitrust/commission restrictions; in MSFT, the filing flags competition, regulation, AI and cloud compliance, and security/data rules; in GOOGL, it flags privacy/data regulation, the DMA, antitrust, and export/data-transfer constraints; in AMZN, it flags trade, tariffs, data/privacy, foreign rules, and regional operating restrictions; in NVDA, it flags export controls, sanctions, AI regulation, and government actions that could block shipments and demand. JPM and LLY do not give the same operationally identical risk in the passages we have here; JPM points the reader back to its broader supervision-and-regulation risk discussion, and LLY only says there have been no material changes to the previously disclosed risk factors. XOM is different again: its filing centers commodity, policy, and geopolitical risk rather than the same tech-platform style regulatory hit.
What that means for the book: this is a correlated issuer-risk cluster, not a sector label. The names that look most exposed to the same-day version of this problem are AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, and NVDA, because their filings all point to rules, enforcement, or government actions that can hit access, distribution, margins, or shipments at once. The evidence we hold does not let me quantify the joint drawdown from that cluster from the filings alone, so I cannot say how much of the book would be taken out on the same day; that would need a portfolio risk run rather than filing text.

turns.q: so what's actually been offsetting anything in here? and if the answer is nothing, what am I really long
turns.answer:
What is offsetting something in here is not a hedge sleeve in the tidy sense; the held book only shows composition, not attribution. The portfolio is 10 holdings as of 2026-09-04, with two fixed-income ETFs inside it: HYG at 7.29% and TLT at 6.06%. That tells us the book is explicitly mixed, but it does not show which line item offset which other line item in a selloff.
So if the question is whether any one sleeve has been proven to offset another, the desk cannot answer that from the held sections it has today: attribution is not held, and drawdown explanation is not held on the path I have. The right absence here is not a nearby figure with the wrong name; it is simply not held as a figure on this desk right now.
If the answer is that no offset has been demonstrated, then what you are really long is the blended return stream of a concentrated equity book with a small rates/credit ballast: AAPL 14.7%, JPM 14.9%, LLY 12.7%, MSFT 16.1%, GOOGL 12.5%, AMZN 7.14%, XOM 4.41%, NVDA 4.24%, plus HYG and TLT. The book also carries concentration warnings in LLY and MSFT, so the real long is not just credit but a tilted mix of equity beta with some fixed-income diversifiers.
What would change this reading is a held attribution or drawdown episode showing that HYG or TLT contributed positively while equities fell, or a market-risk run showing the rates/credit beta of the book. Without that, the only defensible statement is that the portfolio owns those sleeves, not that they have been proven to offset anything.

turns.q: which of the names we own actually say something about customer concentration in their own filings?
turns.answer:
Yes — the names we own that actually say something about customer concentration in their own filings are [10-Q Part II, Item 1A] (AAPL), [10-K Item 8] (GOOGL), [10-K Item 8] (LLY), and [10-K Item 7] (NVDA). Each has filing text that directly addresses concentration or whether no single customer exceeded 10% of revenue.
AAPL says the company depends on carriers and other resellers and notes that a decline in demand for a single product category could materially affect sales; that is concentration risk in the filing, though it is not the same thing as naming a single customer-share figure. GOOGL is the cleanest disclosure: it states that no individual customer or affiliated group represented more than 10% of revenues in 2023, 2024, or 2025. LLY gives a concrete concentration point: its three largest wholesalers each accounted for between 16% and 24% of consolidated revenue. NVDA is explicit that revenue is concentrated among a limited number of direct and indirect customers and gives named-year percentages for direct customers.
The others are either about a different question or do not hold customer-concentration as a filed figure: AMZN’s passages here are segment/product/geography and backlog, not customer concentration; JPM’s passages are about credit-risk concentrations and client coverage, which answers lending/credit concentration rather than revenue customer concentration; KO discusses bottlers and even says one bottler accounted for 10% of net operating revenues, which is concentration but at the bottler/channel level; XOM discusses revenue by geography and contract scope, not customer concentration as asked.
If you want, I can turn this into a name-by-name table with the exact passage id and the concentration statement each filing makes.

turns.q: google's told us what they're doing on capex and where the money's going. has anything they've actually reported since squared with that, or are they saying one thing and the numbers doing another?
turns.answer:
Google’s reported numbers do line up with the capex story on the top line of the cash-flow statement, but the pace has gotten materially heavier. Operating cash flow was $165B (2025-12-31) in 2025-12-31, up from prior years, while capex was $91.45B (2025-12-31) in 2025-12-31, also up sharply. The cash left after capex was $73.27B (2025-12-31) in 2025-12-31, so the company is still generating positive free cash flow, but capex is now taking a much larger share of operating cash flow: 55.5% (2025-12-31) in 2025-12-31 versus lower shares in earlier years. That means the numbers are not contradicting the capex message; they are showing the spending is indeed accelerating.
The comparison that best answers your question is the trend. Capex rose by 74.1% (2025-12-31) in 2025-12-31 on a year-over-year basis, while revenue rose by 13.9% (2024-12-31) in 2024-12-31. So capex growth has been outpacing revenue growth in the reported periods we have. That is the “numbers doing another” part: not a mismatch with management’s capex message, but a faster reinvestment tempo than sales growth.
On cash uses, buybacks were $45.71B (2025-12-31) in 2025-12-31 and dividends paid were $10.05B (2025-12-31) in 2025-12-31. The buyback line has slowed from earlier years, while dividends only began showing up in the more recent periods. So the mix of capital return and investment has shifted toward capex, not away from it.
One caveat: I do not hold a filed depreciation-amortization figure for GOOGL under that exact line name. The desk says that is not held as filed, so I cannot test capex against depreciation with that measure. The available filed figure is depreciation, which answers a different question.

turns.q: and what do they say themselves would knock it off course?
turns.answer:
Yes — in Item 7, Alphabet says the main things that could knock the capex plan off course are the same things that could change the business mix and cash generation: demand, competition, regulation, financing conditions, and the cost/efficiency of AI infrastructure. The clearest capex-specific statement is that they expect to significantly increase, relative to 2025, their investment in technical infrastructure, including servers and network equipment, and data centers. That means the base case is not a slowdown in capex; it is continued expansion unless one of the listed pressures changes the economics.
What they say could push it off that path is, first, weaker or different monetization of AI and other products: they say they may monetize differently than their historical consumer and enterprise offerings, which could affect revenue growth rates and margin trends, and that competition from other AI developers may affect revenues. Second, they say revenue can be affected by foreign currency exchange rates, pricing, general economic conditions, geopolitical events, regulations, new product launches, and seasonality. Third, on the cost side, they note TAC growth, rising compliance and legal costs, and higher infrastructure operating costs, all of which could compress margins or alter capital priorities.
They also flag balance-sheet and financing constraints in a practical way: they say they raised capital through debt in 2025 and may continue to seek debt or other financing in the future, and they continue to enter finance leases, mainly for data centers. So a tighter financing market, or a desire to protect liquidity, is one of the things that could change the pace or shape of the buildout. What would not be a new story from their filings is simple continued heavy capex: that is explicitly the story they are telling.
If you want the one-management-question version, it is: what specific demand, monetization, or infrastructure-efficiency change would make you revise the stated plan to increase technical-infrastructure capex relative to 2025? That is the question the filing leaves open.

turns.q: so what am I actually underwriting when I hold this — give me the thing that has to stay true
turns.answer:
The thing you are underwriting is that Alphabet can keep expanding AI and cloud demand, monetize it in a way that still works economically, and scale technical infrastructure fast enough and efficiently enough that the spend creates value rather than destroys it. The filing says the company expects to significantly increase its technical-infrastructure investment relative to 2025, while also trying to drive data-center efficiencies; the hold case is that those two move together, not against each other.
What has to stay true is the chain the filing lays out: user and customer adoption keeps rising, monetization does not lag too badly as AI products evolve, competition does not overwhelm pricing or share, and financing, regulation, and macro conditions do not force a materially different capital plan. If any of those break, the capex story stops underwriting the earnings story.
So the question is not whether capex stays high; the filing already says it will. The question is whether the incremental dollars in servers, network equipment, and data centers keep earning their way through revenue growth and margin resilience. That is the thing that has to remain true for the position to work.
